summary: Balázs Horváth frames the talk around the question of what AI will not take from software professionals. With code generation no longer the bottleneck, the expensive part of the lifecycle is now getting stakeholders, decision-makers, and subject matter experts into the room to elicit requirements—because, as he puts it, you can prompt your AI but you cannot prompt the room. A VisualLabs internal hackathon illustrates this: 21 agent ideas were generated, 17 were abandoned for lacking data access, a clear business owner, or measurable value, and 4 survived into production. AI by definition produces the most common answer, so relying on it to build faster risks replicating existing solutions—a faster horse rather than a car. Horváth recommends three practical tools. Story mapping captures the process backbone (e.g., contacting, triaging, resolving, closing for a support system) and user stories at the right altitude; MVP stories sit in the first row, backlog items below. User stories should follow the familiar persona/what/need/why format because AI was trained on that structure and performs better with it. A four-question value framework asks: whose problem is this, what does winning look like, what would make them refuse to use it, and what decision does it change. The VAD path (Value → Architecture → Design) ensures design follows process understanding, which follows value understanding. He acknowledges this resembles traditional product management—old skill, new economics. Anti-patterns include high feature velocity with low adoption, treating the demo as the deliverable, and PRDs without real user testers. He recommends shifting KPIs from features shipped to features used more than twice, moving smartest people toward customer-facing roles, and always running a mapping session before building. In closing, he urges the audience to empirically test the value of user stories by building a good use case with and without them and comparing results; his own turning point was realizing he still needs user stories in development, so the team can build the right thing rather than just the next thing. He invites further conversation via a LinkedIn QR code.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Opening: The Bottleneck Has Shifted
sections.summary: Horváth introduces the premise: with code generation no longer the bottleneck, the real challenge is figuring out what to build, which depends on people skills. He references the VisualLabs hackathon (21 ideas, 17 abandoned, 4 in production) and his 13-year career bridging business and IT across ERP and CRM programmes. The shift is that building is cheap; deciding what to build is expensive.

sections.title: AI Produces the Average—Humans Must Move Beyond It
sections.summary: Using Henry Ford's faster-horse analogy, Horváth argues that AI gives the most common answer, so using it to build faster risks replicating existing solutions. The goal is to move from a faster horse to a car—a magnitude shift—by applying analyst toolkit skills like story mapping, business model canvas, and value canvas.

sections.title: Story Mapping in Practice
sections.summary: Story mapping captures the process backbone (contacting, triaging, resolving, closing for a support system) with user stories beneath at high altitude. The first row is the MVP (capture intent, classify urgency, draft grounded answer, log to record); subsequent rows form the backlog. User stories should follow the persona/what/need/why structure because AI was trained on it and performs better with that familiar pattern. Acceptance criteria derive test cases; daisy-chained stories form a coherent system.

sections.title: Four-Question Value Framework and VAD Path
sections.summary: Four questions to elicit value: whose problem is this, what does winning look like, what would make them refuse to use it, and what decision does it change. Answers should be tracked in a markdown file in the repo for AI context. The VAD thinking path (Value → Architecture → Design) ensures you understand value and process before designing. Horváth acknowledges this resembles traditional product management—old skill, new economics—where the differentiator is who understands the business need better.

sections.title: Anti-Patterns and Recommended Shifts
sections.summary: Anti-patterns include high feature velocity with low adoption (people try but do not reuse), demo-as-deliverable, and PRDs without real user testers. Recommended actions: audit and realign metrics, shift from counting features shipped to features used more than twice, move smartest people toward customer-facing roles, involve subject matter experts in build decisions, and always run a mapping session before building.

sections.title: Closing: Build the Right Thing, Not Just the Next Thing
sections.summary: Horváth encourages the audience to try a good use case both with and without user stories and compare the results. His own turning point was realizing he still needs to incorporate user stories in development so the team can build the right thing, not just the next thing. He invites further conversation via a LinkedIn QR code and thanks the audience.

demonstrations: Support system story map example with backbone stages: contacting, triaging, resolving, closing a case; MVP row includes capturing intent, classifying urgency, drafting a grounded answer, logging to system of record; backlog row includes reading sentiment, writing to a team, suggesting next action, checking satisfaction.
Example user story: 'As a support lead, I need to open cases ranked by urgency so that none of the escalations should slip.'
limitations: AI by definition is coded to give the most common answer, risking replication of existing solutions rather than step-change improvement.
A generic prompt like 'build us an agent that handles support' will not get the answer you want without value, architecture, and design context.
Demo systems are not live systems; fast demos do not equate to production adoption.
